title: Worldly right view
hookLine: that giving bears fruit, that deeds matter, that there are good teachers (MN 117)

lines: A GRANDMOTHER WHO NEVER READ A SUTTA.
cards: Six in the morning, a village road, and a grandmother who has never read a sutta is already waiting with a pot of rice for the monks' bowls. She does this every day. She's honest at the market.
She tells her grandchildren that what you do comes back to you, that your parents deserve respect, that there are good people in the world worth listening to.
Does she have right view, or is that only for scholars who can recite the twelve links? The Buddha says there are two kinds of right view. She has the first.

teach.b: The sutta is number one hundred seventeen in the Middle-Length Discourses, the Great Forty. In it the Buddha says right view is twofold.

There's right view still bound up with the world, sharing in merit and ripening in good results. And there's right view that is noble, beyond the world: the wisdom of someone who has entered the path for real.
Then he spells out the worldly kind, as things a person holds to be so.
There is what is given: giving bears fruit. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is this world and the other world.
There is mother and father, which the commentaries read as: they matter, and are owed gratitude. There are beings reborn spontaneously.
And there are good, well-practiced teachers who have seen these things for themselves and make them known.
Not complicated philosophy: basic confidence that actions have consequences, that generosity isn't wasted, that parents and teachers count.
In Pali, the action is kamma, karma in Sanskrit, and its result is vipaka, the ripening.

teach.h: THE GROUND THE NOBLE KIND GROWS FROM.
teach.b: The Buddha doesn't call worldly right view second-rate; teachers often describe it as the ground the noble kind grows from.

And again and again in the same sutta he says right view comes first, because it lets you tell wrong view as wrong and right view as right. So the grandmother with her rice pot isn't doing something less than the scholar.
She's on the first floor of the same house. Modern Buddhists hold different views about rebirth and other worlds, and teachers address that in different ways.
The list's center holds across them: deeds matter.

how: In Theravada lay practice, right view is often lived as confidence in kamma: giving to monks and the needy, honoring parents and teachers, and trusting that good actions bear good fruit.

o: a punishment sent down by a god
the ripening, the result of a deed
the deed itself, the act you do

games.q: match each piece of worldly right view.
p: the wisdom of one on the path

s: in MN 117 the Buddha says right view is twofold
worldly right view, sharing in merit, and noble right view, beyond the world.
worldly right view is dismissed as useless
the sutta counts it as right view; teachers describe it as the ground of the noble kind.
worldly right view includes that mother and father matter
it's on the list, along with giving, deeds and good teachers.

games.q: a grandmother gives rice to monks every morning, is honest at market, and honors her parents. she's never read a sutta. by MN 117, does she have right view?
o: only if she can recite the twelve links.
games.why: MN 117 counts confidence that giving bears fruit and deeds matter as right view: the worldly kind, ground of the noble kind.

practice: Think of one kind thing someone did for you long ago, a teacher who stayed late, a stranger who helped, and notice whether it still lives in you; that's a fruit.
Then think of one small thing you did for someone else, and imagine it ripening in them, quietly, somewhere you'll never see. Let both rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Vipaka, the ripening of an action's result. Worldly right view: giving bears fruit, deeds have results, parents matter, and good teachers exist, the ground of the path.

orig.note: Pali kamma, Sanskrit karma: intentional action; its result is called vipāka, ripening.

carryVoice: Your line: deeds matter. Small kindnesses ripen in places you may never see. See you tomorrow.
